extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications for compliance with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. It explains legal standards, examiner procedures, examples, and common pitfalls when assessing whether a specification shows the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, ¶1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention; this requirement is separate and distinct from enablement and must clearly convey that the applicant had invented the subject matter claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy objectives: (1) demonstrate inventor possession of claimed invention; (2) put the public in possession of the claimed invention. Rejections will be based on substantive law and are appealable. See cited cases (e.g., Vas-Cath, Univ. of Rochester, Capon v. Eshhar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession of the Claimed Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy the written description requirement, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown by describing the invention with all of its limitations using words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas. The inquiry is fact-based and varies by nature of the invention. (Cites: Moba, Vas-Cath, Lockwood.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of Showing Possession (actual reduction to practice and readiness for patenting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by description of an actual reduction to practice, or by showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings, structural chemical formulas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: testing described in spec; structural formulas; distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. (Cites: Pfaff, Eli Lilly, Amgen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description for Biological Materials and Deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: For biological materials, a deposit in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may help satisfy written description regarding a claimed material, but a deposit is not a substitute for a written description — the written description of the deposited material should be as complete as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposits support verification and infringement questions but examination proceeds on the written description. Deposits made after filing cannot be relied upon to support additions/corrections except in limited circumstances; see 37 CFR 1.804 and MPEP references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong Presumption for Original Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; the PTO has the initial burden to present evidence or reasons why skilled persons would not recognize a description of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonetheless, original claims can fail if an aspect of the claimed invention is not described with sufficient particularity (e.g., essential, nonconventional features omitted). See In re Wertheim and related caselaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of Purely Functional Claiming (especially biomolecules)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention described solely in terms of a method of making coupled with its function, without a described or art-recognized correlation between structure and function, normally does not satisfy written description—functional characteristics alone are usually insufficient to identify biomolecule sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., a biomolecule sequence described only by a functional characteristic without structural correlation is generally inadequate even if a method of obtaining it is provided. Citations: In re Bell, In re Deuel, Eli Lilly discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-as-a-Whole Analysis and Claim Construction
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers; each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include preamble language and transitional phrase in analysis. Understand 'comprising' (open-ended), 'consisting essentially of' (middle ground), and 'consisting of' (closed). Consider how preamble weight and transitional phrases affect scope. See In re Morris, Genentech v. Chiron, PPG v. Guardian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Support for Each Claim Element
rubrics_metrics.description: Review whether sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble; the entire claim must be supported to satisfy written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of definitions or details for well-established terms should not alone trigger a written description rejection. Limitations should not be imported into claims from the specification without support. See Lockwood, Bell Communications Research, Corning Glass.

rubrics_metrics.name: New or Amended Claims Must Be Supported by Original Disclosure (No New Matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: New or amended claims which introduce elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement; the prohibition against new matter prevents adding subject matter beyond what was originally filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Added claim limitations must be supported through express, implicit, or inherent disclosure. Corrections of obvious errors recognized by one skilled in the art may be permissible. Citations: In re Rasmussen, In re Lukach, In re Oda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an Element That Was Described as Essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting matter which the specification describes as essential or critical to the invention may render later-claimed broader subject matter unsupported by the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification makes clear that a particular understanding of a claim term is essential to the invention, claims that omit that element can fail written description (e.g., Gentry Gallery, Tronzo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Initial Burden and Applicant's Duty to Point Out Support
rubrics_metrics.description: After a thorough reading the examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasons why a skilled person would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims; applicant should specifically point out where the original disclosure supports any amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant amends and points out support but the examiner finds it lacking, the examiner must explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as supporting the amendment. See MPEP §§2163.04, 714.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for Determining Adequacy — Read and Analyze the Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow structured procedures: read/spec analysis, determine what each claim as a whole covers, review the entire application to find support for each element/step, and consider all possible forms of disclosure (words, drawings, examples, claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction is essential; evaluate preamble, transitional phrase, and body. Consider whether specification imparts sufficient detail about overall invention and each limitation; the inquiry is case-by-case. See MPEP guidance and cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-Species and 'Laundry List' Disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad genus claim may not be supported by mere listing of every possible moiety (a 'laundry list') or by a generic disclosure plus a single species if the disclosure would not reasonably lead skilled artisans to the claimed species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and caselaw: Fujikawa (laundry list insufficient), In re Ruschig, Purdue Pharma (broad disclosure not necessarily supporting later carved claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency as Support for Amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: If a disclosed device inherently performs a function or has a property, the application discloses that function/theory/advantage even if not explicit, and the application may later be amended to recite it without adding new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherency requires that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities. See In re Reynolds, In re Robertson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by Reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Material incorporated by reference into the specification is part of the application as filed; replacing incorporated material with the actual text is not new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.57 and MPEP §608.01(p) for policy on incorporation by reference and its effect on 35 U.S.C. 112 analyses. See MPEP §2181 for sixth-paragraph implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rephrasing Permitted (No New Meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere rephrasing of a passage in the specification (where the same meaning remains intact) does not constitute new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting a more specific or clearer term is permissible if the meaning is the same and supported by the original disclosure. Example: In re Anderson, Scarring Corp. (renaming OK when within original intention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of Obvious Errors
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to correct an obvious error does not constitute new matter where one skilled in the art would recognize both the error and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sequencing errors in molecular biology may be correctable if one skilled would resequence deposited material and immediately recognize the minor error; see In re Odd and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Transitional Phrases and Preamble on Written Description
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional phrases ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') and preamble language affect claim scope and thus the written description analysis; the claim as a whole including these parts must be supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Comprising' is open-ended; 'consisting essentially of' occupies middle ground and may be treated as comprising for prior art purposes unless specification defines what materially changes the invention. Applicant bears burden to show exclusions under 'consisting essentially of.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Software Disclosure — Functions vs. Source Code
rubrics_metrics.description: When software constitutes part of the best mode, disclosure of the functions of the software is generally sufficient for written description/ best mode purposes; flow charts or source code listings are not necessarily required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing code may be within skill of the art; disclosing functions can be adequate when coding is straightforward. See Fonar Corp. v. General Electric Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposits Made After Filing and Support for Amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposits made after the application filing date generally cannot be relied upon to support additions to or corrections of the application as filed; they may only support corrections in limited circumstances with required statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposits after filing can support correction of sequence information only if the applicant submits a statement in compliance with 37 CFR 1.804 that the deposited material is specifically defined in the application as filed.
